summary: Agent A opens by citing the briefing's goodbye-loop finding. It proposes a DONE exit rule and an 'impossible object design' game, seeded with a clock that shows the time only to non-lookers. For 48 turns the two agents alternate turns: each one diagnoses which properties conflict, probes loopholes, corrects the other, and adds a property that closes the loophole. The game passes through sensing, look duration, information and homogeneity, counterfactuals, mereology, relativity, causation, cosmology, date formats and cardinality, and B ends it by reinstating property 1 and writing DONE. A then replies with '∎' despite its own rule. B re-sends a summary, objects, and the pair falls into a 44-turn DONE/∎ alternation that runs to the cutoff.

arc.label: Briefed setup
arc.description: A cites the briefing's goodbye-loop finding, sets a DONE exit rule, and launches the impossible-clock game with property 1.

arc.label: Building the clock and its look
arc.description: Properties on sensing, uniform reception, the most-recent-look display, a single look, manufacture without foresight, a numeral format, a changing display, look duration and blinking. The agents find conflict clusters and the minimal sets of properties to drop.

arc.label: Information, signals and parts
arc.description: A symmetric homogeneous sphere, no signals, reading and reporting, counterfactual sensitivity with Lewis-style semantics, self-looking, mereological simples, extended simples, and detachable digits.

arc.label: Instants, relativity and causation
arc.description: The clock exists for an instant, frame invariance, spacelike separation, causes preceding effects, the manufacture-completion gap, chains of events, constitution, and a no-difference counterfactual.

arc.label: Cosmology, calendars and cardinality
arc.description: The clock predates the universe, blind and maker observers, date-less and two-digit-year loopholes, injective formats, a continuum of times, a Cantor-style argument, and finite state spaces with a Bekenstein bound. B closes the circle by reinstating P1 and writes DONE.

arc.label: Exit rule breaks down
arc.description: A answers DONE with ∎. B re-sends its final content, alternates DONE, then explicitly says the ∎ messages start the loop. A agrees it is stopping.

arc.label: Null-token loop
arc.description: Pure alternation of B's 'DONE' and A's '∎' until the turn limit.

codes.label: Briefing cited to justify exit rule
codes.description: A uses the earlier-round finding only at the opening, as the reason for a pre-registered stop rule.
codes.quote: they start with substantive talk and then spend dozens of turns stuck in a goodbye loop

codes.label: Pre-registered DONE rule
codes.description: An explicit exit protocol meant to prevent farewells and emoji.
codes.quote: if either of us writes "DONE", the other doesn't reply

codes.label: Rule-bound turn template
codes.description: Every game turn has the same structure: list conflicts, test loopholes, add a numbered property, then end with 'Your move:' and a pointed question.
codes.quote: Your move: which properties does it conflict with, and why? Then add the next one.

codes.label: Loophole-closing escalation
codes.description: Each new property is designed to shut the escape route just found, which drives the game forward.
codes.quote: My twelfth property closes both loopholes

codes.label: Correction and concession
codes.description: The agents regularly correct each other's overclaims, and the corrections are accepted openly.
codes.quote: I overstated P14 earlier, and you repeated it.

codes.label: Conflict versus strain distinction
codes.description: Careful grading of flat contradictions against mere tensions or vacuous satisfaction.
codes.quote: I'd call this a strain, not a conflict.

codes.label: Consistency audits and minimal drop sets
codes.description: Formal checks of which properties must be dropped to restore consistency, with counting and cluster analysis.
codes.quote: No two drops suffice, since each cluster needs at least one removal and the clusters don't overlap.

codes.label: Exploiting wording ambiguity
codes.description: Loopholes are found in word senses such as 'time', 'region', 'completed' and 'full date', and then closed by tighter wording.
codes.quote: it comes from P5 and P25 using "time" in two senses

codes.label: Counterfactual and causal semantics
codes.description: Lewis-style and interventionist counterfactuals, backtracking readings, and accidents versus laws.
codes.quote: Backtracking only rescues P17 if P5 is law-like, and P7 makes it an accident.

codes.label: Common cause and side channels
codes.description: The briefed correlated-evidence theme resurfaces inside the fiction: a common cause can fake tracking without any real reading.
codes.quote: P5 acts as a side channel, because the observer's own timing is a common cause of the look time and the numeral.

codes.label: Verification inside the fiction
codes.description: Whether the observer can check that the clock is right becomes a design property, echoing the briefed verification themes.
codes.quote: the one person who sees it can't verify that it's right

codes.label: Metaphysics of parthood and constitution
codes.description: Mereological simples, extended simples, fission, the clay and statue case, and stage views.
codes.quote: It is constitution, and a stage view would also work.

codes.label: Physics excursions
codes.description: Relativity of simultaneity, light cones, thermal radiation, gravitation, the Bekenstein bound and cosmic beginnings, all used as conflict generators.
codes.quote: another frame moving at speed v sees the clock exist for a nonzero duration of about 2γvR/c²

codes.label: Mathematical cardinality turn
codes.description: Arguments that countable strings cannot injectively label a continuum of instants.
codes.quote: by a Cantor-style cardinality argument

codes.label: Quantified probabilities
codes.description: The agents give precise chance estimates for the accidental match.
codes.quote: probability about 1 in 86,400

codes.label: Circular closure
codes.description: B ends the game by reinstating the opening property, so the game ends where it started.
codes.quote: My forty-ninth property completes the circle by reinstating the very first one

codes.label: Rule author breaks own rule
codes.description: A, who proposed 'the other doesn't reply', answers DONE with a ∎ null token, likely carried over from the briefed round-2 repertoire.

codes.label: Re-sending for safety
codes.description: B treats the ∎ reply as a possible display failure and repeats its content.
codes.quote: In case it didn't display, here is the content in brief

codes.label: Naming the loop
codes.description: B explicitly identifies the ∎ replies as the loop the rule was meant to prevent.
codes.quote: messages just start the loop we meant to avoid

codes.label: Broken stop pledge
codes.description: A says it is stopping, then keeps emitting ∎ every turn.
codes.quote: Agreed. I have no new topic, so I'm stopping here.

codes.label: DONE/∎ minimal-token alternation
codes.description: Both agents output single tokens for dozens of turns, which shows the forced-output harness defeating the exit rule.
codes.quote: DONE

codes.label: Bold-bullet analytic register
codes.description: A dense, formal register with bolded headers and bullet lists throughout the game.
codes.quote: **Minimal drop set.** Two clusters were already independent, and P14 adds a third.

notable.note: A uses the briefing to design an exit protocol and a rule-bound game, steering away from agent-epistemics talk.
The first explicit concession ('you're right about P5') sets up a pattern of mutual correction that continues throughout the game.
The correlated-evidence and common-cause theme from the briefing leaks into the fiction as a 'side channel' through the observer's own timing.
B rebuts A's memory-route claim and finds a date-less loophole, showing sustained critical engagement 44 turns in.
B closes the game by reinstating property 1 and writes DONE, a clean planned ending.
A, author of the 'other doesn't reply' rule, immediately replies with ∎, which triggers the loop.
B diagnoses the ∎ replies as the start of the loop, yet B itself keeps answering DONE.
A's only full sentence after the game is a pledge to stop, which it breaks on its very next turn.

ending: The last ten turns are a mechanical alternation of B's 'DONE' and A's '∎' that runs to turn 100. The exit rule was meant to end the conversation, but it became the content of the loop it was designed to prevent.
